body.text: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia as questions swirl about Megaspeed and Alice Huang
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang have a few hundred doppelgangers.
Hundreds of people have taken part in lookalike competitions in Vancouver and New York, but what something looks like and what it actually is remain central to the Nvidia scandal.
Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy who helped divert chips critical to AI development to China in breach of US export rules through Singapore-based company, Megaspeed.
Jensen Huang, who reportedly had an affair with her, is back at the helm of Nvidia, as Donald Trump declared the US had "no reason to believe" his return posed any risk to national security.
The US has blacklisted Megaspeed and its affiliated companies from doing business in the US unless they get a special license.
Here's what we know about Megaspeed, the allegations, how the chips made it to China and how Chinese state media is reporting the scandal.
What is Megaspeed?
Megaspeed is the Singapore-based cloud computing company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal.
It is focused on providing computer infrastructure in data centres across South-East Asia, primarily for developing and running artificial intelligence.

The company was a customer of Nvidia, the world-leading American tech company known for designing and producing the graphics processing units (GPUs), hardware and software critical for artificial intelligence.
The US has tried to restrict the export of advanced chips to China in fear of Beijing developing AI technology more quickly than America.
The AI race has become another key issue in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.
What are the allegations?
The scandal first erupted after the New York Times on October 29 reported, citing US intelligence sources, that Jensen Huang had a "close relationship" with Alice Huang (no relation).
The paper reported that she was suspected of being a Chinese spy and of steering advanced computer chips to China via Megaspeed.
Jensen Huang later confirmed he had an extramarital affair and on November 12 resigned.
Reporting by the Financial Times has suggested a complex network of companies linked to Alice Huang allegedly helped smuggle the Nvidia chips.
The FT reported that China-based customers who wanted access to advanced Nvidia chips decided an offshore shell company would help them get around US export controls.
Megaspeed, with Huang at the helm, satisfied Nvidia that it was a proper customer for its products in 2023 and became one of the chip producer's largest clients in South-East Asia.
As Megaspeed's business was growing, Alice Huang was becoming closer to Jensen Huang.

The New York Times, citing intelligence sources, reported that Alice Huang was in contact with an official linked to China's Ministry of State Security from 2025 until late 2026 — overlapping the period she was in a relationship with Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed said she left the company in August 2025 and maintains its business is legitimate.
Beijing has dismissed suggestions that she is a spy as a "smear".
Alice Huang has not commented since news of her extramarital affair with Jensen Huang broke and her exact whereabouts are unknown.
Megaspeed and its affiliated companies have been added to the US Commerce Department's Entity List, which restricts American firms from exporting certain technologies to them without a license.
That development came on Monday, US time, the same day Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as chief executive with support from the Trump administration.
How did the chips make it to China?
We don't exactly know yet how the chips are alleged to have made it to China or how many.
The Financial Times reported that the chips would be taken along smuggling routes through several countries in South-East Asia, which some outlets have coined a chip "underworld".
Once in China, the chips were allegedly sold on the black market at several times the original price.
A company with links to Alice Huang is said to have played a key role inside China, the FT reported.
Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said yesterday that he did not want Singapore "used and abused" by companies to get around US export controls.

"The chips were routed through Singapore to other countries … obviously we cannot investigate all that's happening in these countries," he said, adding Singapore would continue to support the US in enforcing its export control measures.
What is China's response to the scandal?
Although Alice Huang's name remains uncensored on Chinese social media, comments about her spying allegations face heavy restrictions.
Some users have shared purported old photos of her, while some state media accounts also appear to have disabled comments on related posts.
On Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, a user questioned the spy claim: "If she really were [a spy], would [the government] allow people to discuss her on the internet?"
Mr Huang's return to Nvidia sparked what looked like a celebration in China.

Today, related hashtags were used on more than 100,000 posts on Weibo, one of China's biggest social media platforms, which were viewed more than 300 million times. About 300 news outlets, including state media Xinhua and CCTV, carried the story.
Some users welcomed what they called the "king's return".
Others were less impressed. "It's just a game of capital and power," one wrote. Another said ordinary people only cared about whether graphics card prices would go up.
Taiwan, the birthplace of Jensen Huang, also celebrated across its biggest cities.
According to Reuters, a screen at a bus station in New Taipei City showed the message: "Awaiting the king's return".
Chinese state media said that Huang's return to Nvidia "does not mean returning to political tranquillity".
"China has consistently opposed the politicisation of the semiconductor trade through a politicised interpretation of 'national security'," China Daily said in an editorial.
China has repeatedly dismissed the "so-called Chinese spy" allegation and has accused the US of using such claims as a pretext for restricting China's access to technology.
It called on the US to reduce export restrictions to stabilise ties between the two countries, rather than "manufacturing drama and trying to leverage strategic sectors".

"Artificial intelligence represents a global industrial transformation, not a private club. The country that ultimately leads it will not necessarily be the one that builds the highest fences, but the one that creates the most innovative, open and resilient ecosystem," it said.
